doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

chapter: Kai and J.J., Bohemia and Embers
title: House rhythm section at Cafe Bohemia and Tony Scott's early records
summary: Playing at the Bohemia with Pettiford and Kenny Clarke, and how Johnny Mandel taped the Tony Scott Quartet for Bob Thiele.

bands.name: Kai Winding and J.J. Johnson group

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: No. I worked with them a lot in the old Half Note, I used to work down there. And let’s see, you want to point me, now let’s see after, oh yeah, the best job I had, after I left Kai and J.J. and was freelancing with everybody, I played with — I was in the house rhythm section at the Café Bohemia with Oscar Pettiford and Kenny Clarke. That was one of the greatest experiences. And we used to have different horn players — Art Farmer, Donald Byrd, Gigi Gryce.

Jerome Richardson, Gigi Gryce, one weekend it was Miles. And that rhythm section, that’s the best I ever had anything to do with. Those two people were — now on Tony’s first record we did — well the first one — well I’m going to back up a little bit. I wish they’d reissue those records. One night up at Minton’s the first time we were there with the three, a guy who I befriended named Johnny Mandel, who was one of these guys, he played jazz bass trumpet and he used to write arrangements for Elliot Lawrence and all different people. He was in that — Al Cohn, Tiny Kahn, all these great guys. Johnny one night brought his — he had a professional tape machine he lugged around. Concord that’s what it was, a big reel to reel. He lugged it all the way up to Minton’s and he recorded us, the Tony Scott Quartet. So Tony took the tapes to the late Bob Thiele, you heard that name?
Who is running Brunswick. And he put it out on ten inch. I still have it, it’s a real souvenir, that was my first.
Yeah. Then we went in the studio. Then the next year we went back there with Osie Johnson and Earl May who’s still out here.
I saw him recently. And you ought to interview him.
I did. He’s a good guy.
